subject: chemistry
title: Structure and bonding of carbon
welcome_lead: Today's adventure: Structure and bonding of carbon — AQA GCSE Chemistry (8462) specification, section 4.2.3.
meta_desc: GCSE Chemistry (AQA) practice covering Structure and bonding of carbon, specification section 4.2.3.
final_note: You worked through Structure and bonding of carbon — 12 specification statements.

concepts.def: A form of carbon in which each carbon atom forms four covalent bonds with other carbon atoms in a giant covalent structure. Diamond is very hard, has a very high melting point and does not conduct electricity.
A structure in which very many atoms are joined to one another by covalent bonds in a continuous network, so that there are no separate molecules. Diamond and graphite are giant covalent structures.
A shared pair of electrons between two atoms. Covalent bonds are strong, so a great deal of energy is needed to break the many covalent bonds in a giant covalent structure.
A form of carbon in which each carbon atom forms three covalent bonds with three other carbon atoms, forming layers of hexagonal rings which have no covalent bonds between the layers.
A ring of six carbon atoms. The layers in graphite, and the sheet in graphene, are built from hexagonal rings of carbon atoms.
An electron that is not held in a bond between two particular atoms and is free to move through the structure. In graphite, one electron from each carbon atom is delocalised.
A single layer of graphite. Its properties make it useful in electronics and composites.
A molecule of carbon atoms with a hollow shape. The structure of fullerenes is based on hexagonal rings of carbon atoms but they may also contain rings with five or seven carbon atoms.
The first fullerene to be discovered, C₆₀, which has a spherical shape.
A cylindrical fullerene with a very high length to diameter ratio. Carbon nanotubes are useful for nanotechnology, electronics and materials.
How many times longer a shape is than it is wide. Carbon nanotubes have very high length to diameter ratios: they are extremely long compared with how narrow they are.
A material made by combining two materials so that the mixture has properties neither has alone. Graphene and carbon nanotubes are added to composites to strengthen them.

mcqs.q: In diamond, how many covalent bonds does each carbon atom form, and with what?
options: Four covalent bonds, with four other carbon atoms
Four covalent bonds, to atoms of other elements
Four covalent bonds, inside a small molecule
Three covalent bonds, to other carbon atoms
mcqs.explain: The specification states that in diamond each carbon atom forms four covalent bonds with other carbon atoms.

mcqs.q: Which set of properties does diamond have?
options: Very hard, low melting point, does not conduct
Very hard, very high melting point, does not conduct
Very hard, very high melting point, conducts electricity
Soft and slippery, high melting point, conducts
mcqs.explain: These are exactly the three properties of diamond given by the specification.

mcqs.q: Explain why diamond has a very high melting point.
options: The weak forces between diamond's molecules must be overcome
The delocalised electrons hold the carbon atoms in place
Many strong covalent bonds have to be broken to melt it
Its carbon molecules are heavy, so more energy is used
mcqs.explain: Diamond is a giant covalent structure, so melting it means breaking very many strong covalent bonds.

mcqs.q: Explain why diamond does not conduct electricity.
options: Covalent bonds between its layers stop electrons moving
Its delocalised electrons cannot move through the structure
It has no ions, and only ions can carry a current in a solid
All four outer electrons of each carbon are in bonds
mcqs.explain: With every outer electron used in a covalent bond, diamond has no delocalised electrons to carry charge.

mcqs.q: In graphite, how many other carbon atoms is each carbon atom bonded to, and how are the atoms arranged?
options: Four others, in layers built from rings of six atoms
Three others, in layers built from rings of six carbon atoms
Three others, in a giant three-dimensional network
Three others, in rings of five joined into a hollow ball
mcqs.explain: The specification states three covalent bonds per carbon atom, forming layers of hexagonal rings.

mcqs.q: What does the specification say about bonding between the layers in graphite?
options: Strong covalent bonds join each layer to the next
The delocalised electrons form covalent bonds between layers
There are no covalent bonds between graphite's layers
Each layer shares pairs of electrons with the next
mcqs.explain: The specification says the layers of hexagonal rings have no covalent bonds between the layers.

mcqs.q: How many electrons from each carbon atom in graphite are delocalised?
options: All four of the outer electrons of every carbon atom
Two electrons from each atom, leaving 2+ ions in the sea
None: every electron in graphite is in a bond
One electron from each carbon atom is delocalised
mcqs.explain: The specification states that in graphite one electron from each carbon atom is delocalised.

mcqs.q: Explain why graphite is soft enough to leave a mark on paper.
options: Layers slide off because no covalent bonds join them
Its covalent bonds are weak, so the structure crumbles
Its delocalised electrons let the carbon atoms slide past
Graphite melts at a low temperature and rubs away easily
mcqs.explain: With no covalent bonds between the layers, whole layers slide over one another and rub off.

options: Its carbon atoms move along the layers carrying charge
Ions in graphite are free to move between the layers
One delocalised electron per carbon atom can move through it
Each carbon has a spare electron held in a covalent bond
mcqs.explain: One electron from each carbon atom is delocalised, and delocalised electrons are free to move.

mcqs.q: In what way is graphite similar to a metal?
options: It can be hammered into new shapes without breaking
It is held together by strong ionic bonds, as metals are
It is built from positive ions in a sea of electrons
It contains delocalised electrons that are free to move
mcqs.explain: The specification says graphite is similar to metals in that it has delocalised electrons.

options: A single layer of graphite, exactly one atom thick
A stack of several graphite layers bonded firmly together
A hollow ball of carbon atoms, like Buckminsterfullerene
A giant carbon structure with four bonds per atom
mcqs.explain: The specification defines graphene as a single layer of graphite.

mcqs.q: Graphene is useful in electronics. Which explanation of this uses graphene's structure and bonding correctly?
options: It conducts, because its weak covalent bonds free the electrons
It conducts: each carbon has a delocalised electron
It does not conduct: all four outer electrons are in bonds
It conducts, because it is a hollow cage that traps ions
mcqs.explain: Graphene is a single layer of graphite, so one electron from each carbon atom is delocalised and free to move.

mcqs.q: Which statement about Buckminsterfullerene is correct?
options: It is a giant covalent structure with the formula C₆₀
It is a solid ball of carbon, with the formula C₆₀
It is a flat sheet of carbon with the formula C₆₀
It is a hollow, spherical molecule with the formula C₆₀
mcqs.explain: The first fullerene to be discovered was Buckminsterfullerene (C₆₀ ), which has a spherical shape.

mcqs.q: A structure is described as a hollow cage of carbon atoms built from hexagonal rings together with some rings of five carbon atoms. What is it?
options: A fullerene, as its cage can contain rings of five atoms
Graphene, because a graphene sheet is a hollow carbon cage
Diamond, because its rings can hold five carbon atoms
Graphite, because its layers curl into hollow cages
mcqs.explain: Fullerenes are hollow molecules based on hexagonal rings that may also contain rings of five or seven carbon atoms.

mcqs.q: Which description fits a carbon nanotube?
options: A solid rod of pure carbon with a very high length to diameter ratio
A cylindrical fullerene with a very high length to diameter ratio
A sphere of carbon atoms with a very high length to diameter ratio
A tube of diamond with a very high length to diameter ratio
mcqs.explain: The specification describes carbon nanotubes as cylindrical fullerenes with very high length to diameter ratios.

mcqs.q: Which of these is a use of fullerenes, including carbon nanotubes?
options: Cutting and drilling hard rock, as they are the hardest
Lining furnaces, as they melt at a very high temperature
Strengthening composites and use in electronics
Making pencil leads slide smoothly across the paper
mcqs.explain: The specification names nanotechnology, electronics and materials as uses of carbon nanotubes.
